ann_113.text: Through this part, older age clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less only while age stays below about 35 years: for a typical person, going from 19 to 90 years moves it from about 95% to about 62%.
So being 58 rather than 22 years old clearly lowers it from about 93% to about 62%, with no further change past that age.

ann_114.text: Through this part, more capital gains clearly lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, slowly at first, then faster: for a typical person, from about 62% with no gains to about 6% with gains of $6,849, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower.

ann_115.text: Through this part, technical support work lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 52% (on the training data only).
Being born in Guatemala or having a missing country of birth slightly raises it, to about 65% (on the training data only).

ann_116.text: Through this part, being Asian or Pacific Islander rather than White slightly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 62% to about 58% (on the training data only).

ann_117.text: Through this part, working as a handler or cleaner clearly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 76%.
A doctorate lowers it to about 52% (on the training data only).
Being born in Cambodia also lowers it to about 52%, but the model has little data on this (19 people), on the training data only.

ann_118.text: This part acts on the 187 of 39,073 people in the training data whose occupation is private household service, and 185 of them had an income of $50,000 or less.
Through it, private household service raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 87% (on the training data only).

For the typical person it acts on (a 43-year-old White woman, never married and not in a family, a high-school graduate in private household service in the private sector, born in the United States, working 35 hours a week), it slightly raises the predicted chance from about 99% to above 99% (on the training data only).

ann_119.text: This part acts on the 96 of 39,073 people in the training data born in China, and 68 of them had an income of $50,000 or less.
Through it, being born in China raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 62% to about 85% (on the training data only).

For the typical person it acts on (a 40-year-old Asian or Pacific Islander man born in China, married to a civilian spouse, with a bachelor's degree and a professional specialty job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week), it raises the predicted chance from about 22% to about 49% (on the training data only).

ann_120.text: For a typical person, the model clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily as the education scale rises from 7 to 13 (about 89% to 24%, flattening out near the top at low education because it cannot go much higher), with capital losses of $1,887 (to about 29%) and as weekly hours rise from 24 to 55 (about 71% to 52%).

It clearly lowers it slowly at first, then faster with capital gains (about 62% at none to 6% at $6,849, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower), and steadily with age up to about 34 years, then no further (about 93% at 22 years to 62% at 58).

Compared with a husband, it clearly gives a wife a lower chance (about 27%) and someone's own child (about 94%) or any other household relationship (about 84%) a higher one; any marital status other than married to a civilian spouse (about 87%) and being a woman (about 80%) clearly raise it.

Compared with a professional specialty, private household service (about 87%), farming or fishing (about 83%), other service (about 81%) and handlers or cleaners (about 76%) clearly raise it, and executive or managerial jobs (about 49%), protective service (about 49%) and technical support (about 53%) clearly lower it.

On the training data only, a highest education of 1st-4th grade (about 10%), 7th-8th grade (about 19%), 12th grade without a diploma (about 48%) or a doctorate (about 52%) and federal government work (about 51%) lower it, while a missing work class (about 79%), self-employment without incorporation (about 77%), state government (about 73%) and local government work (about 69%) raise it.

Country of birth also moves it (on the training data only): being born in Ireland (about 26%), Portugal (about 36%), England (about 51%) or Cuba (about 57%) lowers it, and being born in Vietnam (about 87%), China (about 85%), the Dominican Republic (about 82%), Haiti (about 74%), Hong Kong or India (about 72%) or Japan (about 70%) raises it.

Being born in Scotland raises it to about 88%, and being born in Honduras (about 43%), Cambodia (about 52%) or Hungary (about 54%) lowers it, but the model has little data on this (14 to 19 people each), on the training data only.

ann_113.original: Hypothesis: a youth bonus to P(<=50K). Age enters only via the ReLU hinge 599=relu(-1.763*age-0.494), active below z=-0.280 (~35 years, using est. mean 38.6/sd 13.7 y). 8375 and 3328 are always active, so they are linear relays and the contribution collapses to 1.258*relu(-1.763*age-0.494)+0.463: flat (0.463) at 35+ years, +0.161 logit per year younger, 3.335 at age 17. Evidence: closed form from get_formula; line plot on full train (n=39073) shows the hinge, corr -0.78; local ablation AUC 0.9078->0.9002. Supported.
ann_113.proposed: Being younger raises the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, but only below about 35 years of age; above that age makes no difference through this part.

ann_114.original: Hypothesis: capital gain's whole effect, a concave piecewise-linear penalty on P(<=50K). Contribution = -2.787*cg - 3.581*relu(0.8175*cg-0.453): slope -2.79 per sd below z=0.554 (~5.2k USD), -5.71 per sd above it. +0.41 logit at cg=0 (95% of rows), -9.0 at the 99th pct, -73.7 at 99,999 USD (output saturated to ~0). ann_114.proposed: More capital gains lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less.

ann_115.original: Hypothesis: small per-category offsets for occupation:13 (inferred Tech-support) and two rare countries. ann_116.original: Hypothesis: a small negative offset for race:1 (inferred Asian-Pac-Islander), -0.149 logit relative to others, via the direct edge. The race:4 (White) gate 9712 and the gate 5394 are dead on train (0% active; bias outweighs every reachable input), contributing a constant 0. Evidence: closed form; sensitivity zero for race:4; ablation AUC unchanged. Supported; the gates are dead code.

ann_117.original: Hypothesis: a three-level categorical offset. Gate 5993=relu(1.861-0.453*edu10+0.605*occ6-0.729*nc1) is relayed linearly by 7165 (always active) into the output with weight 0.294. ann_120.original: Hypothesis: the network is an additive logistic model. logit P(<=50K) = 0.776 + sparse linear backbone over 40 direct inputs + sum of 7 child contributions, then sigmoid. Backbone (direct edges, standardised inputs): education-num -1.41, marital-status:2 (Married-civ-spouse) -0.73, relationship:5 (Wife) -0.56, relationship:0 (Husband) -0.56, relationship:3 (Own-child) +0.43, sex (Male) -0.42, hours-per-week -0.33, capital-loss -0.30, plus small workclass/occupation/education/country offsets. Children: capital_gain_penalty (concave piecewise-linear, kink ~5.2k USD), youth_hinge (+0.16 logit per year below ~35), and five near-inert categorical gates (Handlers-cleaners/Doctorate relay, Tech-support, Priv-house-serv, China, Asian-Pac offset). The children have no multiplicative interactions; they meet only at the output sum. 54 one-hot inputs are unconnected (zero effect); native-country:15 is constant in train; four hidden nodes (9712, 5394, 12643, 2197) never activate. Evidence: closed form (get_formula); train acc 0.852, AUC 0.908 (n=39073); local mean-ablations: backbone AUC->0.748, capital gain ->0.890, age ->0.900, each gate costs <=0.0003 AUC; KernelSHAP (200 train samples) top mean|SHAP|: education-num 0.105, marital-status:2 0.068, relationship:0 0.054, identity_age 0.046, identity_capgain 0.040, sex 0.026. Supported.
ann_120.proposed: A higher education level, capital gains and losses, longer hours, older age and being a wife lower the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less; being someone's own child, not being married to a civilian spouse, being a woman and service, farming or manual jobs raise it.

summary.text: For a typical person (a 37-year-old White man married to a civilian spouse, born in the United States, a high-school graduate in a professional specialty job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week with no capital gains or losses), a higher education level clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily, from about 89% at 7 to about 24% at 13 on the 1-16 scale (flattening out near the top at low education because it cannot go much higher), and capital gains clearly lower it slowly at first, then faster, from about 62% at none to about 6% at $6,849, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower.

Compared with a husband, the model clearly gives a wife a lower chance (about 27%) and someone's own child (about 94%) or any other household relationship (about 84%) a higher one, and any marital status other than married to a civilian spouse clearly raises it to about 87%.
Through one part of the model, older age clearly lowers the chance only while age stays below about 35 years: for a typical person, going from 19 to 90 years moves it from about 95% to about 62%.

Being a woman clearly raises it to about 80%, while capital losses and longer working hours clearly lower it steadily: to about 29% at $1,887 of losses, and from about 71% at 24 hours a week to about 52% at 55.
Private household service (about 87%), farming or fishing (about 83%) and other service jobs (about 81%) clearly raise it compared with a professional specialty.
A highest education of 1st-4th grade (about 10%) or 7th-8th grade (about 19%) lowers it compared with the education categories the model groups with high-school graduates (on the training data only).
